cards.front: What happens to the double bonds of alkene monomers during addition polymerisation?
cards.back: The **double bonds open** and each monomer joins its neighbours to form a chain. Nothing is lost, so the polymer is the only product.
cards.hint: Think about what the bond between the two carbons becomes as monomers link.

cards.front: Why does condensation polymerisation release a second product, unlike addition polymerisation?
cards.back: Each link forms when two **functional groups** react, releasing a small molecule, usually water. Addition polymerisation has no such step.
cards.hint: Think about what happens at the two ends of each monomer when they react.

cards.front: Why are polyamide fibres usually stronger than polyester fibres?
cards.back: Polyamide chains have **hydrogen bonds** between N-H and C=O groups on neighbouring chains. Polyesters have no N-H groups, so only weaker dipole-dipole forces act between their chains.
cards.hint: Compare the groups present in each polymer's chain.

cards.back: The **smallest section of a polymer chain** that repeats along its length.

cards.front: What steps turn an alkene monomer into its repeating unit?
cards.back: Change the C=C **double bond to a single bond**, keep the two former double-bond carbons in the main chain, place side groups above and below, then add open bonds and brackets with $n$ outside.
cards.hint: Start by looking at the double bond in the monomer.

cards.front: What is the repeating unit of poly(propene)?
cards.back: $[{-}CH(CH_3){-}CH_2{-}]_n$, with the **CH3 group** as a side group hanging off the main chain.
cards.hint: Draw propene first, then convert its double bond.

cards.front: A student says condensation polymerisation gives only the polymer. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: This is wrong. Condensation always releases a **small molecule**, such as water, at each link, while addition polymerisation gives only the polymer.
cards.hint: Compare with what addition polymerisation produces.

cards.back: A compound with a **carboxyl group at each end** of its carbon chain.

cards.front: Which link forms when a diol reacts with a dicarboxylic acid?
cards.back: An **ester link**, $-COO-$, formed as water is lost from each hydroxyl and carboxyl pair.
cards.hint: Each hydroxyl group reacts with a carboxyl group.

cards.front: Why can polyesters be broken down more easily than addition polymers?
cards.back: Their ester links are **polar** and can be hydrolysed by water, and acids or alkalis speed this up. Addition polymers have no such weak points.
cards.hint: Compare the bonds in the chain with the carbon-carbon bonds of addition polymers.

cards.front: Which link joins the monomers in a polyamide?
cards.back: An **amide link**, $-CONH-$, formed when an amine group reacts with a carboxyl group and water is lost.
cards.hint: Think about the end groups of the diamine.

cards.front: Why is nylon-6,6 named as it is?
cards.back: Each monomer, hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid, has **six carbon atoms**, which gives the name.
cards.hint: Count the carbons in each monomer's name.

cards.front: Why do addition polymers persist in the environment?
cards.back: They have **strong carbon-carbon bonds** and no polar groups for water to attack, so they are not biodegradable.
cards.hint: Think about what water or microorganisms could attack.
